platforms.title: Why Is My Blood Pressure Higher at the Doctor's Than at Home?
platforms.meta_description: High at the clinic but normal at home? What white coat and masked hypertension mean, which setup errors add points, and CDC steps for a reliable home reading.
platforms.body_html:
You check your blood pressure at the kitchen table and see 122/78. Two days later the nurse reads 146/92 and your doctor mentions medication. Which number is real? According to the CDC, up to 1 in 3 people with a high reading at the doctor's office may have normal readings elsewhere, a pattern often called white coat syndrome. That doesn't mean the office number is wrong, or that your home number is automatically right. It means a single reading in an exam room is a snapshot, and you need a better picture before anyone decides what to do.

Why does the number change between the clinic and your kitchen?

The most common reason is the setting itself. Being rushed into an exam room, sitting on the edge of a table, chatting with the nurse and feeling nervous about the visit can all raise your pressure for a few minutes. When the office reading is high but readings taken at home or with a 24-hour ambulatory monitor are normal, clinicians call it white coat hypertension.

The opposite also happens, and it's easier to miss. In masked hypertension, your blood pressure looks fine at the clinic but runs high during ordinary life, at work, after a stressful commute, or in the early morning. Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline (Whelton and colleagues, published in Hypertension), a daytime home average of 130/80 mmHg or higher corresponds to the office cutoff for stage 1 hypertension. If your office numbers are normal but your home average sits at or above that line, that's the pattern your doctor will want to know about.

The third reason is technique, and it affects both settings. A tip sheet from the federal Million Hearts initiative, adapted from American Medical Association and Johns Hopkins material, lists how much common positioning errors can add to a reading: a cuff over clothing can add 5 to 50 mmHg, talking or active listening about 10, an unsupported arm about 10, a full bladder about 10, crossed legs 2 to 8, an unsupported back and feet about 6, and a cuff that's too small 2 to 10. These are estimates, not exact corrections, but they show how easily a careless reading at home or in a busy clinic can drift away from your true pressure.

Skip the one-off checks, here's what gives a reliable home reading

The CDC's home measurement steps are short, and following them every time matters more than any single trick:

  • Don't eat or drink anything for 30 minutes beforehand. Smoking, alcohol, caffeine and exercise in that window can also raise the reading.
  • Empty your bladder first.
  • Sit in a comfortable chair with your back supported for at least 5 minutes, both feet flat on the floor and legs uncrossed.
  • Rest your cuffed arm on a table at chest height, with the cuff on bare skin, snug but not too tight.
  • Don't talk while the monitor is working.
  • Take at least two readings, 1 or 2 minutes apart, at the same time every day, and write them down.

The device matters too. Pick an automatic monitor with a cuff that goes around your upper arm rather than your wrist or finger, make sure the cuff fits your arm, and look for a model that has been clinically validated for accuracy. A practical check is to bring your monitor to your next appointment and compare it with the office device, so you know whether your home numbers line up.

One reading on a good day or a bad day won't settle anything. A useful log covers several days, with readings in the morning and evening, so your clinician can look at the average instead of reacting to one high or low number. Note anything unusual next to a reading, such as poor sleep, pain or a missed dose, because it helps explain outliers.

So which number should you believe?

Neither on its own. The office reading still matters, and white coat hypertension isn't something to simply ignore, which is why your doctor may keep checking it over time. But a consistent set of home readings, taken the same careful way each time, shows what your blood pressure does in the life you actually live. That's often what decides whether treatment is needed or working.

If you remember one thing, make it the setup: a bare arm, an empty bladder, a supported back and five quiet minutes turn your home monitor from a rough guess into evidence your doctor can use.

Sources: CDC, Measuring Your Blood Pressure; Million Hearts, 7 Simple Tips to Get an Accurate Blood Pressure Reading (adapted from AMA and Johns Hopkins); Whelton PK et al., 2017 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults, Hypertension, 2018.
